title: Chemical eye injury (acid and alkali burns)
subject: ophthalmology-ent
summary: Irrigate immediately and copiously (at least 30 minutes, or longer until the conjunctival pH is 7.0 to 7.5 five minutes after stopping), remove trapped particles from the everted lids and fornices, then grade limbal and conjunctival damage (Roper-Hall or Dua) and refer urgently to ophthalmology. Alkali injuries are usually worse than acid.

sections.title: Irrigate first
items: Start irrigation at once, before history-taking or visual acuity: at the scene use any clean tap water; in hospital use normal saline or Ringer lactate (Ringer lactate or balanced salt solution cause less corneal oedema).
Instil topical anaesthetic (for example proparacaine 0.5%) to relieve blepharospasm; use a lid speculum or irrigating lens, and irrigate both eyes if both are exposed.
Irrigate for at least 30 minutes; severe alkali injuries may need very large volumes (up to 20 L or more). Do not try to neutralise with an acid or alkali.
Evert the upper lid (double eversion) and sweep the fornices with moistened cotton buds to remove particles such as lime or cement, which keep releasing alkali.
Check conjunctival pH with litmus paper: pause about 5 minutes after irrigating and retest; continue until pH is 7.0 to 7.5 and stays there.

sections.title: Assess and grade
items: History: the agent (check the container label), time of exposure, first aid given, and whether particles were involved.

Alkalis (lime, cement, plaster, ammonia, drain cleaners, firecrackers) penetrate deeply by saponification and are usually worse. Acids (battery acid, toilet cleaners) coagulate surface proteins and penetrate less, except hydrofluoric acid.

After irrigation: visual acuity, fluorescein staining for epithelial defects, extent of limbal ischaemia (clock hours), percentage of conjunctival involvement, corneal clarity, anterior chamber reaction, and IOP.

Roper-Hall: grade I epithelial damage, no limbal ischaemia (good prognosis); II corneal haze with iris visible, under one-third limbal ischaemia (good); III stromal haze obscuring iris, one-third to one-half ischaemia (guarded); IV opaque cornea, over one-half ischaemia (poor).

Dua: grade I no limbal or conjunctival involvement; II up to 3 clock hours and up to 30% conjunctiva; III over 3 to 6 hours, 30 to 50%; IV over 6 to 9 hours, 50 to 75%; V over 9 to under 12 hours, 75 to under 100%; VI total limbus and conjunctiva (very poor).
A white, quiet-looking eye after a severe alkali burn may reflect limbal ischaemia, not a mild injury.

sections.title: Refer
items: Refer every chemical injury with an epithelial defect, corneal haze, limbal ischaemia, raised IOP or reduced vision urgently to ophthalmology (same day); moderate to severe injuries need specialist care from the start.
Grade III and above (Roper-Hall) or Dua grade III and above: manage in a cornea service where amniotic membrane and limbal procedures are available.
Hydrofluoric acid, large-volume or facial burns, or inhalational injury: involve toxicology and burns teams.

sections.title: Acute medical treatment (ophthalmology)
items: Preservative-free topical antibiotic until the epithelium heals, and a cycloplegic for pain and iritis.

Topical steroid (prednisolone acetate 1% or dexamethasone 0.1%) intensively in the first 7 to 10 days to control inflammation, then taper; longer use only with close specialist monitoring because of corneal melting.
Anti-collagenase and healing support for moderate to severe injury: oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, oral vitamin C 1 to 2 g daily, topical ascorbate 5 to 10% and topical sodium citrate 10%.
Raised IOP: oral acetazolamide is preferred; avoid adrenergic agents (they worsen limbal ischaemia).
Preservative-free lubricants frequently; bandage contact lens or amniotic membrane transplantation for moderate injuries (Dua II to III) to speed epithelial healing.
Give analgesia; do not send the patient home with topical anaesthetic drops.

sections.title: Children and medico-legal
items: Children often need restraint, sedation or examination under anaesthesia to irrigate adequately and to inspect the fornices; do not accept inadequate irrigation.
Avoid doxycycline in children under 8 years and in pregnancy.

Acid attack (assault) injuries in India: treat as a medico-legal case, document carefully with photographs and inform police; free treatment is mandated for survivors. Look for facial, airway and skin burns.
Common Indian sources: lime (chuna) sachets and whitewash, cement, firecrackers during festivals, Holi colours, battery acid and toilet cleaners.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying irrigation to find sterile fluid, take a history or measure acuity.
Stopping irrigation too early, or testing pH immediately after irrigating (the reading reflects the irrigating fluid).
Missing retained particles under the upper lid or in the fornices.
Underestimating a white eye with limbal ischaemia after alkali injury.
Continuing intensive topical steroid beyond 10 to 14 days without specialist review.

drugs.name: Proparacaine 0.5% (or tetracaine) eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 drops before and during irrigation as needed
drugs.notes: For irrigation only; never for home use.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.notes: Anti-collagenase; avoid under 8 years and in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 g orally daily in adults
drugs.notes: For moderate to severe alkali injury; topical 5 to 10% ascorbate and 10% sodium citrate drops are added by ophthalmology.

drugs.name: Acetazolamide
drugs.dose: 250 mg orally up to four times daily for raised IOP in adults
